sections.h2: Where to record a deed in Yavapai County
sections.html:
The Yavapai County Recorder takes deeds at two counters. One is in Prescott, the county seat, at 1015 Fair Street, Room 228, Prescott, AZ 86305. The other is in Cottonwood at 10 S 6th Street, Cottonwood, AZ 86326.

Call (928) 771-3244, option 6, for Prescott or (928) 639-5807 for Cottonwood. Questions can also go to web.recorder@yavapaiaz.gov.

The office records real estate transactions, mortgages, deeds of trust, family trusts, and subdivision plats and surveys. For a house sale, the document that matters is the deed, plus any release of the old mortgage or deed of trust that your title company records at the same time.

Every instrument costs one flat $30.00. Inside that price are the affidavit of property value, added indexing, the state surcharge and postage for the return trip, so you will not see a pile of extra line items on a typical deed. The recording fee increase rests on A.R.S. 11-475.

Call the Recorder before you send a check, since the county revises its fee sheet from time to time.

sections.h2: What must be attached to a deed
sections.html:
An affidavit of legal value travels with most deeds. A.R.S. 11-1133 says a title-transferring deed carries a Department of Revenue form signed by seller and buyer or their agents. An incomplete form means the recorder has to turn the deed away, except when an exemption notation appears on the deed.

What the form asks for:

  • Each party's name, mailing address and phone number, plus the address for the tax statement
  • Legal description in full, the property's street address and the assessor's parcel number
  • Sale date, total price, cash down payment and how the buyer is financing
  • Any personal property in the deal that is worth five percent or more of the price
  • Intended use of the home, such as owner-occupied or rented

A.R.S. 11-1134 lets some transfers skip the form: a gift deed, a conveyance ordered by a court, a quitclaim given for no money, and residential transfers for nominal consideration between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings. The person claiming an exemption writes it on the front of the instrument.

sections.h2: Recording or ordering copies without a visit
sections.html:
Only one of the ways to deal with the Recorder requires a trip to the counter. Each path has its own rules, so pick the one that fits the timing of your closing.

  • Web recording. An online portal runs through Tyler Technologies (tylertech.com/webrecording). You register for an account and submit documents from home or an office.
  • In person. Walk the document into the Prescott or Cottonwood counter.
  • Self-service search. Recorded documents can be searched online on the county website.
  • Mail for copies. Send a written request or the county's official copy request form to Yavapai County Recorder, 1015 Fair St, Room 228, Prescott, AZ 86305. Add a self-addressed stamped envelope big enough for the order, and write the check to Yavapai County Recorder.

The Recorder's forms page also carries a copy request form, commercial and non-commercial record request forms, a Social Security number redaction form and a DD-214 military discharge request form.

The median single-family sales price in the county is $539,000 for sales recorded through October, down 2.9 percent from $555,000 in 2025. A recorded deed is what feeds that sales data, so an accurate affidavit helps keep the county's numbers clean.

Yavapai County spans many towns and districts, including Prescott, Prescott Valley, Cottonwood, Camp Verde, Clarkdale, Jerome and Wickenburg. School districts include Prescott Unified, Humboldt Unified, Chino Valley Unified, Camp Verde Unified, Sedona Unified and Mingus Union High School. Check which district your address falls in before you name one in a listing.

sections.h2: Recorded documents, tax liens and your bill
sections.html:
A recorded deed leaves a tax lien in place. A.R.S. 42-17153 makes the property tax lien arise on January 1 of the tax year, and it remains until taxes, penalties, charges and interest are paid. State liens and liens for other years' taxes come first; the property tax lien outranks other liens and encumbrances.

For that reason the title company requests a payoff from the Yavapai County Treasurer before closing. When a house sells before the bill arrives, the new owner or mortgage company pays that current-year bill, though taxes already due stay with the current owner. Bills are mailed by the end of September. Per A.R.S. 42-18052, a first-half payment is late after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 and a second-half payment after 5:00 p.m. on May 1, so a closing between those dates should settle whichever installment is open.

Homestead protection is automatic and limited. It is covered in A.R.S. 33-1101 through 33-1105, and an attorney can explain how it applies to your own situation, since the Recorder's office cannot give legal advice.

sections.h2: How a Yavapai County sale moves to recording
sections.html:
For a seller, the paperwork follows a set order. The title company searches the record for liens, you and the buyer sign the deed and the affidavit, funds are released, and the deed goes to the Recorder, either by web recording or at a counter.

Bring photo identification and your payoff statements to the signing. If your deed qualifies for an exemption, check that the exact exemption is written on its face before it is filed, because the recorder must refuse an incomplete affidavit. After recording, a certified copy is available for $1.00 a page plus $3.00 per certification.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Yavapai County?
faqs.a: One flat $30.00 per instrument, with the affidavit of property value, added indexing, the state surcharge and return postage all included. Public agencies paying from public funds are charged $15.00. Phone (928) 771-3244, option 6, to verify the amount first if you are mailing a check.

faqs.q: Does Yavapai County charge a transfer tax on a home sale?
faqs.a: The recorder's fee sheet carries a single $30.00 instrument charge. Your title company or the Recorder can say if anything further applies to your deed. The A.R.S. 11-1133 affidavit is required, and its cost is already inside the $30.00.

faqs.q: Can I record a Yavapai County deed online?
faqs.a: Yes. An online web-recording portal through Tyler Technologies lets you register for an account and submit documents. Title and escrow companies usually handle this step for a sale, but individual owners can also use it.

faqs.q: Which deeds do not need the affidavit of legal value?
faqs.a: Those exempted by A.R.S. 11-1134, for example gift deeds, court-ordered conveyances, no-money quitclaims and some nominal-consideration transfers among close relatives. The exemption must be written on the deed itself before recording.

faqs.q: How do I get a certified copy of my Yavapai County deed?
faqs.a: Use the county's official copy request form or a written request, mail it to Yavapai County Recorder, 1015 Fair St, Room 228, Prescott, AZ 86305, and include a self-addressed stamped envelope. Expect $1.00 per page for copies and $3.00 for every certification. You can also ask at the Prescott or Cottonwood counter.
